problem: Consider the curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-{y}^{3}=-8.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{12}$ on the curve at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.

examples.knowledge_point: Using an Implicitly Defined Curve to Determine a Second Coordinate
examples.problem: Consider the curve $x^3-\ln y=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$   $y=y(t),$  and that $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ on the curve at the point where $x=1,$ find the value of $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}$ at that point.
examples.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 3{x}^{2}-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}=2$ and $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We also want to substitute for $y,$ but we are not given this value. However, we can find it by substituting $x=1$ into the equation of the curve.

At the point where $x=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $y=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{1}{1} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Consider the hyperbola $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2}=1.$ Given that $x=x(t),$ $y=y(t),$ and that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6$ on the curve at the point $(2\sqrt{3},\sqrt{3}),$ find the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ at that point.
feedback.worked_solution:
Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2} & =1 \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot (\frac{2x}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=6,$ $x=2\sqrt{3},$ and $y=\sqrt{3},$ and solve $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ We get  

$$
\begin{aligned}6\cdot (\frac{2(2\sqrt{3})}{3})-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot (2(\sqrt{3})) & =0 \\ -2\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-8\sqrt{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
